title: GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to beat Googlers' code golf records
author: bjin
snippet: Back in 2015, when I was still at Google, there was a small group of code-golf enthusiasts spending hours trying to save just one byte on their solutions for weekly code-golf problems. No matter how hard you tried, there always seemed to be another Googler who found a shorter…
excerpt: Back in 2015, when I was still at Google, there was a small group of code-golf enthusiasts spending hours trying to save just one byte on their solutions for weekly code-golf problems. No matter how hard you tried, there always seemed to be another Googler who found a shorter solution. And once a problem entered the challenge phase and every solution became public, it was always astonishing to read how brilliant other people's solutions were. 11 years later, LLMs are evolving fast. A recent OpenAI post ("Perplexity and Intelligence", described researchers watching a model solve open math problems one after another in a Slack thread. I started to wonder: how would frontier models compete with the records that a small group of brilliant minds created with hours of effort each week? So I built this benchmark. Frontier models do find a lot of new approaches (and very brilliant ones) to solve these problems. For example, in two problems ("Surviving Queens" and "The Rolling Dice"), frontier models use complex numbers to solve them in Python and Ruby (both languages have built-in complex number support). And for the "(-5)-Smooth Numbers" problem, where you have to write code to list the first n positive integers of the form (-2)^x⋅(-3)^y⋅(-5)^z, most solutions build them with nested loops or by growing a set, then sort. GPT-6.2 Astra gets them all from powers of 4, and earns a sole best with this brilliant solution: g=lambda n:sorted(4**i%(2**999-5)%(2**49-3)for i in range(7000))[:n] There is a dedicated section for this: It's nice to see GPT-6.2 Astra become the first frontier model to beat the human records in code golfing. Along with other frontier models, it finds a lot of interesting solutions that Googlers back in 2015 didn't. On the other hand, I also believe code golfing can be a good benchmark (not a comprehensive one, of course) for frontier models. Code golfing rewards thinking differently, because a shorter solution usually comes from looking at the problem…

title: Show HN: Taskless, turn AGENTS.md and PR comments into runnable checks
author: codedrift_
snippet: Hey HN, I'm Jakob, the solo dev and founder behind Taskless. I got tired of my AGENTS.md files being ignored or forgotten a half dozen turns into conversations. I also remembered reading someone here on HN saying we weren't using nearly enough syntax trees in our code checks…
excerpt: Hey HN, I'm Jakob, the solo dev and founder behind Taskless. I got tired of my AGENTS.md files being ignored or forgotten a half dozen turns into conversations. I also remembered reading someone here on HN saying we weren't using nearly enough syntax trees in our code checks. This is the result. Taskless gives you powerful syntax tree tools with human verifiable fixtures. The CLI is MIT licensed, so running the CLI, onboarding, rule writing, and running the underlying ast-grep & Vale checks are all local. You can give it a try with: npx @taskless/cli and then asking your agent to "onboard with Taskless". Under the hood, the CLI works with your agent to read your PR review comments, fixup commits, and agent files. It takes things that keep recurring and turns them into the simplest code-level enforcement that can prevent the issue going forward. By choosing code over an LLM for the runtime, there's no model once code is generated. The checks can then be committed to your codebase and enforced. I'm particularly proud of how determinism is mixed into the onboarding flow. Any time the CLI can give the agent information without letting the agent wandering the codebase, the CLI does. It results in a more consistent experience with far fewer errors. Anonymous telemetry can be disabled outright by setting DO_NOT_TRACK=1 or TASKLESS_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 in your environment (it collects CLI version, OS, the repo's org/owner, and a bit about the repository it's running in). When the agent's done, it creates a report you can share around to show everyone there's a better way to control the output of agentic coding tools. I thought I'd include a few here from some of my favorite repos. - Effect: I specifically liked Effect because effect-bot is in the PRs fixing bugs and writing docs for the team, and they already use oxlint plugins and a TypeScript language service plugin. - Sentry: Sentry's all open source, and David Cramer's tweeted a lot about determinism, especially now…

author: memalign
snippet: Inspired by JSFiddle, I wondered if it'd be possible to make a mobile-optimized experience where I can paste in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript (generated by my favorite LLM) and run that mini web app with ease. It is possible! Introducing MemFiddle, a way to preview and test simple…
excerpt: Inspired by JSFiddle, I wondered if it'd be possible to make a mobile-optimized experience where I can paste in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript (generated by my favorite LLM) and run that mini web app with ease. It is possible! Introducing MemFiddle, a way to preview and test simple web apps right in your web browser. You can also add MemFiddle to your home screen as a PWA. To get started, prompt your favorite LLM (such as ChatGPT) to give you 'HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript with no dependencies' and then paste the resulting file content into MemFiddle. I created MemFiddle after I convinced my 4-year-old to poop in an unfamiliar place by making a “poop app” together (one-shotting it with ChatGPT on my phone while under duress).
